To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

driver sub-groups based on self-reported behaviour and skill differed significantly in registered offences but not in accidents, and that the sub-group "violating unsafe drivers" had an increased risk for having a traffic offence.
the DBQ and the DSI are suitable instruments for predicting registered traffic law offences, while the subgroups did not differ in accidents.
the DBQ and the DSI are useful instruments for identifying driver sub-groups at risk for traffic offences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying sub-groups of drivers with high risk of traffic offences and the factors that are predictive of traffic offences.
a more detailed understanding of the relationship between self-reported driving behaviour, traffic law violations, and accidents.
the use of self-reports to predict traffic offences and the identification of sub-groups of risky drivers, and is thus relevant for the development of road safety interventions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a self-reported driving behavior profile is a good indicator of traffic law offences but not accidents, and that the profile is predictive of traffic offences.

self-reported driving behaviour profiles are not a very good indicator of police-registered traffic law offences, and that the most predictive factors for police registered traffic offences are having a criminal record, being a man, living without a life partner, and being a self-employed person.
the DBQ and the DSI are useful instruments for identifying drivers at risk of traffic offences, while they are less useful for identifying drivers with a risk of being involved in accidents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the self-reported driving behaviour is a valid and reliable predictor of registered traffic law offences.
the self-reported driving behaviour of a driver is a good indicator for his/her risk for committing a traffic offence.
self-reported driving behaviour can be used as a predictor of traffic law offences, while accidents are not related to self-reported driving behaviour, at least in a Danish context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
driver sub-groups can be identified based on self-report and that these sub-groups differ significantly in traffic offences, but not in accidents.
the DBQ and the DSI can be used in combination with other data to identify sub-groups of drivers at high risk of traffic offences.
the self-reported DBQ and DSK are valid instruments for the prediction of traffic offences.
